The small-QTQ_{T} representations in Eqs. (13) and (14) can be used to compute fixed-order particle distributions in the phase-space slicing method. In this method, we choose a small QTQ_{T} value QTs​e​pQ_{T}^{sep} in the range of validity of Eqs. (13) and (14). If the actual QTQ_{T} in the computation exceeds QTs​e​pQ_{T}^{sep}, we calculate the differential cross section using the full 2→32\rightarrow 3 matrix element. When QTQ_{T} is smaller than QTs​e​pQ_{T}^{sep}, we calculate the event rate using the small-QTQ_{T} asymptotic approximation A⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)A(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) and 2→22\rightarrow 2 phase space. Hence, the lowest bin of the QTQ_{T} distribution is approximated in the NLO prediction by its average value in the interval 0≤QT≤QTs​e​p0\leq Q_{T}\leq Q_{T}^{sep}, computed by integration of the asymptotic approximations.

The phase-space slicing procedure is sufficient for predictions of observables inclusive in QTQ_{T}, but not of the shape of d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} distributions. The latter goal is met by all-orders summation of singular asymptotic contributions with the help of the Collins-Soper-Sterman (CSS) method [16, 17, 11]. The small-QTQ_{T} resummed cross section is denoted as W⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)W(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) and given by a two-dimensional Fourier transform of a function W~​(Q,b,y,Ω∗)\widetilde{W}(Q,b,y,\Omega_{*}) that depends on the impact parameter b→\vec{b}:

W⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)\displaystyle W(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) =\displaystyle= ∫d​b→(2​π)2​ei​Q→T⋅b→​W~​(Q,b,y,Ω∗)\displaystyle\int\frac{d\vec{b}}{(2\pi)^{2}}e^{i\vec{Q}_{T}\cdot\vec{b}}\widetilde{W}(Q,b,y,\Omega_{*}) (15)
≡\displaystyle\equiv ∫d​b→(2​π)2​ei​Q→T⋅b→​W~p​e​r​t​(Q,b∗,y,Ω∗)​e−ℱN​P​(Q,b).\displaystyle\int\frac{d\vec{b}}{(2\pi)^{2}}e^{i\vec{Q}_{T}\cdot\vec{b}}\widetilde{W}_{pert}(Q,b_{*},y,\Omega_{*})e^{-{\cal F}_{NP}(Q,b)}.

In this equation, W~​(Q,b,y,Ω∗)\widetilde{W}(Q,b,y,\Omega_{*}) is written as a product of the perturbative part W~p​e​r​t​(Q,b∗,y,Ω∗)\widetilde{W}_{pert}(Q,b_{*},y,\Omega_{*}) and the nonperturbative exponent exp⁡(−ℱN​P​(Q,b)),\exp\left(-{\cal F}_{NP}(Q,b)\right), which describe the dynamics at small (b≲1​ GeV−1b\lesssim 1\mbox{ GeV}^{-1}) and large (b≳1​ GeV−1b\gtrsim 1\mbox{ GeV}^{-1}) impact parameters, respectively. The purpose of the variable b∗b_{*} is reviewed below.

If QQ is large, the perturbative form factor W~p​e​r​t\widetilde{W}_{pert} dominates the integral in Eq. (15). It is computed at small bb as

W~p​e​r​t​(Q,b,y,θ∗)\displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{pert}(Q,b,y,\theta_{*}) =\displaystyle= ∑aΣa​(θ∗)S​ha2​(Q,θ∗)​e−𝒮a​(Q,b)\displaystyle\sum_{a}\frac{\Sigma_{a}(\theta_{*})}{S}h_{a}^{2}(Q,\theta_{*})e^{-\mathcal{S}_{a}(Q,b)} (16)
×\displaystyle\times [𝒞a/a1⊗fa1/h1]​(x1,b,μ)​[𝒞a¯/a2⊗fa2/h2]​(x2,b,μ).\displaystyle\left[\mathcal{C}_{a/a_{1}}\otimes f_{a_{1}/h_{1}}\right](x_{1},b;\mu)\left[\mathcal{C}_{\bar{a}/a_{2}}\otimes f_{a_{2}/h_{2}}\right](x_{2},b;\mu).

The “hard-vertex” function Σa​(θ∗)​ha2​(Q,θ∗)\Sigma_{a}(\theta_{*})h_{a}^{2}(Q,\theta_{*}) is the normalized cross section for the Born scattering a​a¯→γ​γa\bar{a}\rightarrow\gamma\gamma, with a=u,u¯,d,d¯,…a=u,\bar{u},d,\bar{d},... in q​q¯→γ​γq\bar{q}\rightarrow\gamma\gamma, and a=a¯=ga=\bar{a}=g in g​g→γ​γgg\rightarrow\gamma\gamma. The Sudakov exponent

𝒮a​(Q,b)=∫C12/b2C22​Q2d​μ¯2μ¯2​[𝒜a​(C1,μ¯)​ln⁡(C22​Q2μ¯2)+ℬa​(C1,C2,μ¯)]\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{a}(Q,b)=\int_{C_{1}^{2}/b^{2}}^{C_{2}^{2}Q^{2}}\frac{d\bar{\mu}^{2}}{\bar{\mu}^{2}}\left[\mathcal{A}_{a}\left(C_{1},\bar{\mu}\right)\ln\left(\frac{C_{2}^{2}Q^{2}}{\bar{\mu}^{2}}\right)+\mathcal{B}_{a}\left(C_{1},C_{2},\bar{\mu}\right)\right] (17)

is an integral of two functions 𝒜a​(C1,μ¯)\mathcal{A}_{a}\left(C_{1},\bar{\mu}\right) and ℬa​(C1,C2,μ¯)\mathcal{B}_{a}\left(C_{1},C_{2},\bar{\mu}\right) between momentum scales C1/bC_{1}/b and C2​QC_{2}Q, and C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are constants of order c0≡2​e−γE=1.123​…c_{0}\equiv 2e^{-\gamma_{E}}=1.123... and 11, respectively. The symbol [𝒞a/a1⊗fa1/h]​(x,b,μ)\left[\mathcal{C}_{a/a_{1}}\otimes f_{a_{1}/h}\right](x,b;\mu) stands for a convolution of the kT−k_{T}-integrated PDF fa1/h​(x,μ)f_{a_{1}/h}(x,\mu) and Wilson coefficient function 𝒞a/a1​(x,b,C1/C2,μ)\mathcal{C}_{a/a_{1}}(x,b;C_{1}/C_{2},\mu), evaluated at a factorization scale μ\mu and summed over intermediate parton flavors a1a_{1}:

[𝒞a/a1⊗fa1/h]​(x,b,μ)\displaystyle\left[\mathcal{C}_{a/a_{1}}\otimes f_{a_{1}/h}\right](x,b;\mu) ≡\displaystyle\equiv ∑a1[∫x1d​ξξ​𝒞a/a1​(xξ,b,C1C2,μ)​fa1/h​(ξ,μ)].\displaystyle\sum_{a_{1}}\left[\int_{x}^{1}{\frac{d\xi}{\xi}}\mathcal{C}_{a/a_{1}}\left(\frac{x}{\xi},b;\frac{C_{1}}{C_{2}},\mu\right)f_{a_{1}/h}(\xi,\mu)\right]. (18)

We compute the functions ha,h_{a}, 𝒜a\mathcal{A}_{a}, ℬa\mathcal{B}_{a} and 𝒞a/a1\mathcal{C}_{a/a_{1}} up to orders αs,\alpha_{s}, αs3,\alpha_{s}^{3}, αs2,\alpha_{s}^{2}, and αs,\alpha_{s}, respectively, corresponding to the NNLL accuracy of resummation. The perturbative coefficients at these orders in αs\alpha_{s} are listed in Appendix A.

The subleading contribution from the nonperturbative region b≳1​ GeV−1b\gtrsim 1\mbox{ GeV}^{-1} is included in our calculation using a revised “b∗b_{*}” model [18], which provides excellent agreement with pTp_{T}-dependent data on Drell-Yan pair and ZZ boson production. In this model, the perturbative form factor W~p​e​r​t​(Q,b∗,y,Ω∗)\widetilde{W}_{pert}(Q,b_{*},y,\Omega_{*}) in Eq. (15) is evaluated as a function of b∗≡b/(1+b2/bm​a​x2)1/2,b_{*}\equiv b/(1+b^{2}/b_{max}^{2})^{1/2}, with bm​a​x=1.5​ GeV−1b_{max}=1.5\mbox{ GeV}^{-1}. The factorization scale μ\mu in [𝒞⊗f]\left[{\mathcal{C}}\otimes f\right] is set equal to c0​b−2+Qi​n​i2c_{0}\sqrt{b^{-2}+Q_{ini}^{2}} , where Qi​n​iQ_{ini} is the initial scale of order 1 GeV in the parameterization employed for fa/h​(x,μ)f_{a/h}(x,\mu), for instance, 1.3 GeV for the CTEQ6 PDFs [19]. We have W~p​e​r​t​(b∗)=W~p​e​r​t​(b)\widetilde{W}_{pert}(b_{*})=\widetilde{W}_{pert}(b) at b2≪bm​a​x2,b^{2}\ll b_{max}^{2}, and W~p​e​r​t​(b∗)=W~p​e​r​t​(bm​a​x)\widetilde{W}_{pert}(b_{*})=\widetilde{W}_{pert}(b_{max}) at b2≫bm​a​x2b^{2}\gg b_{max}^{2}. Hence, this ansatz preserves the exact form of the perturbative form factor W~p​e​r​t​(Q,b,y,Ω∗)\widetilde{W}_{pert}(Q,b,y,\Omega_{*}) in the perturbative region of small bb, while also incorporating the leading nonperturbative contributions (described by a phenomenological function ℱN​P​(Q,b)\mathcal{F}_{NP}(Q,b)) at large bb.

The form of ℱN​P​(Q,b)\mathcal{F}_{NP}(Q,b) found in the global pTp_{T} fit in Ref. [18] suggests approximate independence of ℱN​P​(Q,b)\mathcal{F}_{NP}(Q,b) from the type of q​q¯q\bar{q} scattering process. It is used here to describe the nonperturbative terms in the leading q​q¯→γ​γq\bar{q}\rightarrow\gamma\gamma channel. We neglect possible corrections to the nonperturbative contributions arising from the final-state soft radiation in the q​gqg channel and additional S\sqrt{S} dependence affecting Drell-Yan-like processes at x≲10−2x\lesssim 10^{-2} [20], as these exceed the accuracy of the present measurements at the Tevatron. The experimentally unknown ℱN​P​(Q,b)\mathcal{F}_{NP}(Q,b) in the g​ggg channel is approximated by ℱN​P​(Q,b)\mathcal{F}_{NP}(Q,b) for the q​q¯q\bar{q} channel, multiplied by the ratio CA/CF=9/4C_{A}/C_{F}=9/4. This choice is motivated by the fact that the leading Sudakov color factors 𝒜a(k){\cal A}_{a}^{(k)} in the g​ggg and q​q¯q\bar{q} channels are proportional to CA=3C_{A}=3 and CF=4/3C_{F}=4/3, respectively. The uncertainties in the γ​γ\gamma\gamma cross sections associated with ℱN​P​(Q,b)\mathcal{F}_{NP}(Q,b) are investigated numerically in Ref. [3].

In the region QT∼QQ_{T}\sim Q, collinear QCD factorization at a finite fixed order in αs\alpha_{s} is applicable. In order to include non-singular contributions important in this region, we add to W⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)W(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) the regular piece Y⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗),Y(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}), defined as the difference between the NLO cross section P⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)P(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) and its small-QTQ_{T} asymptotic approximation A⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)A(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}):

d​σ​(h1​h2→γ​γ)d​Q​d​QT2​d​y​d​Ω∗\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma(h_{1}h_{2}\rightarrow\gamma\gamma)}{dQ\,dQ_{T}^{2}\,dy\,d\Omega_{*}} =\displaystyle= W⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)+P⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)−A⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)\displaystyle W(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*})+P(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*})-A(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) (19)
≡\displaystyle\equiv W⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)+Y⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗).\displaystyle W(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*})+Y(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}).

At small QT,Q_{T}, subtraction of A⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)A(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) in Eq. (19) cancels large initial-state radiative corrections in P⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗),P(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}), which are incorporated in their resummed form within W⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)W(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}). At QTQ_{T} comparable to QQ, A⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)A(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) cancels the leading terms in W⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)W(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}), but higher-order contributions remain from the infinite tower of logarithmic terms that are resummed in WW. In this situation the W+YW+Y cross section drops below the finite-order result P⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)P(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) at some value of QTQ_{T} (referred to as the crossing point) in both the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg and g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channels, for each QQ and yy. We use the W+YW+Y cross section as our final prediction at QTQ_{T} values below the crossing point, and the NLO cross section PP at QTQ_{T} values above the crossing point.

A few comments are in order about our resummation calculation. The hard-vertex contribution Σa​(θ∗)​ha2​(Q,θ∗)\Sigma_{a}(\theta_{*})h_{a}^{2}(Q,\theta_{*}) and the functions ℬa​(C1,C2,μ¯)\mathcal{B}_{a}\left(C_{1},C_{2},\bar{\mu}\right) and 𝒞a/a1​(x,b,C/C2,μ)\mathcal{C}_{a/a_{1}}(x,b;C/C_{2},\mu) can be varied in a mutually compensating way while preserving the same value of the form factor WW up to higher-order corrections in αs\alpha_{s}. This ambiguity, or dependence on the chosen “resummation scheme” [21] within the CSS formalism, can be employed to explore the sensitivity of theoretical predictions to further next-to-next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic (NNNLL) effects that are not accounted for explicitly.

The perturbative coefficients in Appendix A are presented in the CSS resummation scheme [11], our default choice in numerical calculations, and in an alternative scheme by Catani, de Florian and Grazzini (CFG) [21]. In the original CSS resummation scheme, the ℬ{{\cal B}} and 𝒞{{\cal C}} functions contain the finite virtual NLO corrections to the 2→22\rightarrow 2 scattering process, whereas in the CFG scheme the universal ℬ{\mathcal{B}} and 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} depend only on the type of incident partons, and the process-dependent virtual correction is included in the function hah_{a}. The difference between the CSS and CFG schemes is numerically small in γ​γ\gamma\gamma production at both the Tevatron and the LHC [3].

In the g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} scattering channel, the unpolarized resummed cross section includes an additional contribution from elements of kTk_{T}-dependent PDF spin matrices with opposite helicities of outgoing gluons [3]. The NLO expansion of this spin-flip resummed cross section generates the term proportional to Σg′​(θ∗,φ∗)∝cos⁡2​φ∗\Sigma_{g}^{\prime}(\theta_{*},\varphi_{*})\propto\cos 2\varphi_{*} in the small-QTQ_{T} asymptotic cross section, cf. Eq. (14). Although the logarithmic spin-flip contribution must be resummed in principle to all orders to predict the φ∗\varphi_{*} dependence in the g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channel, it is neglected in the present work in view of its small effect on the full γ​γ\gamma\gamma cross section.

When integrated over QTQ_{T} from 0 to scales of order QQ, the resummed cross section becomes approximately equal to the finite-order (NLO) cross section, augmented typically by a few-percent correction from integrated higher-order terms logarithmic in QTQ_{T}. Inclusive observables that allow such integration (e.g., the large-QQ region of the γ​γ\gamma\gamma invariant mass distribution) are approximated well both by the resummed and NLO calculations. However, the experimental acceptance constrains the range of the integration over QTQ_{T} in parts of phase space and may break delicate cancellations between integrable singularities present in the finite-order differential distribution. In this situation (e.g., in the vicinity of the kinematic cutoff in d​σ/d​Qd\sigma/dQ discussed in Sec. III) the NLO cross section becomes unstable, while the resummed cross section (free of discontinuities) continues to depend smoothly on kinematic constraints. We see that the resummation is essential not only for the prediction of physical QTQ_{T} distributions in γ​γ\gamma\gamma production, but also for credible estimates of the effects of experimental acceptance on distributions in the diphoton invariant mass and other variables.

II.3 Final-state photon fragmentation

II.3.1 Single-photon fragmentation

In addition to the QCD singularities associated with initial-state radiation [described by the asymptotic terms in Eqs. (13) and (14)], other singularities arise in the 𝒪⁡(αs){\mathcal{O}}(\alpha_{s}) process q⁡(p1)+g⁡(p2)→γ⁡(p3)+γ⁡(p4)+q⁡(p5)q(p_{1})+g(p_{2})\rightarrow\gamma(p_{3})+\gamma(p_{4})+q(p_{5}) [Fig. 1 (e)] when a photon is collinear to the final-state quark. In this limit, the q​g→q​γ​γqg\rightarrow q\gamma\gamma squared matrix element grows as 1/sγ​51/s_{\gamma 5}, when sγ​5→0s_{\gamma 5}\rightarrow 0, where sγ​5s_{\gamma 5} is the squared invariant mass of the collinear γ​q\gamma q pair. In this limit, the squared matrix element factors as

|ℳ⁡(q​g→q​γ​γ)|2≈2​e2​ei2sγ​5​Pγ←q​(z)​|ℳ⁡(q​g→q​γ)|2|{\mathcal{M}}(qg\rightarrow q\gamma\gamma)|^{2}\approx{\frac{2e^{2}e_{i}^{2}}{s_{\gamma 5}}}P_{\gamma\leftarrow q}({z})|{\mathcal{M}}(qg\rightarrow q\gamma)|^{2} (20)

into the product of the squared matrix element |ℳ⁡(q​g→q​γ)|2\left|{\mathcal{M}}(qg\rightarrow q\gamma)\right|^{2} for the production of a photon and an intermediate quark, and a splitting function Pγ←q​(z)=(1+(1−z)2)/zP_{\gamma\leftarrow q}(z)=(1+(1-z)^{2})/z for fragmentation of the intermediate quark into a collinear γ​q\gamma q pair. In Eq. (20) zz is the light-cone fraction of the intermediate quark’s momentum carried by the fragmentation photon, and e​eiee_{i} is the charge of the intermediate quark. When the photon-quark separation Δ​r=(η5−ηγ)2+(φ5−φγ)2\Delta r=\sqrt{(\eta_{5}-\eta_{\gamma})^{2}+(\varphi_{5}-\varphi_{\gamma})^{2}} in the plane of pseudorapidity η=−log⁡(tan⁡(θ/2))\eta=-\log(\tan(\theta/2)) and azimuthal angle φ\varphi in the lab frame is small, as in the collinear limit, sγ​5≈ET​γ​ET​5​Δ​r2,s_{\gamma 5}\approx E_{T\gamma}E_{T5}\Delta r^{2}, where ET​γE_{T\gamma} and ET​5E_{T5} are the transverse energies of the photon and quark, with ET≡E​sin⁡θE_{T}\equiv E\sin\theta. Note that ET​5=QTE_{T5}=Q_{T} at the order in αs\alpha_{s} at which we are working. Therefore, contributions from the final-state collinear, or fragmentation, region are most pronounced at small Δ​r\Delta r and relatively small QT.Q_{T}.11 1 In the soft, or E5→0,E_{5}\rightarrow 0, limit, the final-state collinear contribution is suppressed, reflecting the absence of the soft singularity in the q​g→q​γ​γqg\rightarrow q\gamma\gamma cross section.

A fully consistent treatment of the initial- and final-state singularities would require a joint initial- and final-state resummation. In the approaches taken to date, the fragmentation singularity may be subtracted from the direct cross section and replaced by a single-photon “one-fragmentation” contribution q+g→(q⟶f​r​a​gγ)+γq+g\rightarrow(q\stackrel{{\scriptstyle frag}}{{\longrightarrow}}\gamma)+\gamma, where “(q⟶γf​r​a​g)(\stackrel{{\scriptstyle frag}}{{q\longrightarrow\gamma}})” denotes collinear production of one hard photon from a quark, described by a function Dγ​(z,μ)D_{\gamma}(z,\mu) at a light-cone momentum fraction zz and factorization scale μ\mu. Single-photon “two-fragmentation” contributions arise in processes like g+g→(q⟶f​r​a​gγ)+(q¯⟶f​r​a​gγ)g+g\rightarrow(q\stackrel{{\scriptstyle frag}}{{\longrightarrow}}\gamma)+(\bar{q}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle frag}}{{\longrightarrow}}\gamma) and involve convolutions with two functions Dγ​(z,μ)D_{\gamma}(z,\mu) (one per photon). The lowest-order Feynman diagrams for the one- and two-fragmentation contributions are shown in Figs. 1(f) and 1(g), respectively. Parameterizations must be adopted for the nonperturbative functions Dγ​(z,μ)D_{\gamma}(z,\mu) at an initial scale μ=μ0\mu=\mu_{0}. This is the approach followed in the DIPHOX calculation [14], in which the sum of real and virtual NLO corrections to direct and single-γ\gamma fragmentation cross sections is included. When explicit fragmentation function contributions are included, the inclusive rate is increased by higher-order contributions from photon production within hadronic jets. However, much of the enhancement is suppressed by isolation constraints imposed on the inclusive photon cross sections before the comparison with data. Nevertheless, fragmentation contributions surviving isolation may be moderately important in parts of phase space.

An infrared-safe procedure can be formulated to apply isolation cuts at each order of αs\alpha_{s} [22, 23, 24]. This procedure encounters difficulties in reproducing the effects of isolation on fragmentation contributions, because theoretical models reflect only basic features of the experimental isolation and may introduce new logarithmic singularities near the edges of the isolation cones.

As mentioned in the Introduction, the magnitude of the fragmentation contribution depends on the values of isolation parameters ETi​s​o,E_{T}^{iso}, Δ​R\Delta R, and Δ​Rγ​γ\Delta R_{\gamma\gamma}, modeled only approximately in a theoretical calculation. The collinear approximation constrains from below the values of zz accessible to Dγ​(z,μ)D_{\gamma}(z,\mu): z>zm​i​n≡(1+ET​5i​s​o/ET​γ)−1z>z_{min}\equiv(1+E_{T5}^{iso}/E_{T\gamma})^{-1}. If Dγ​(z,μ)D_{\gamma}(z,\mu) varies rapidly with zz, the fragmentation cross section is particularly sensitive to the assumed values of ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} and zm​i​nz_{min}. For instance, if Dγ​(z,μ)∼1/zD_{\gamma}(z,\mu)\sim 1/z, the fragmentation cross section is roughly proportional to ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} under a typical condition ETi​s​o/ET​γ≪1E_{T}^{iso}/E_{T\gamma}\ll 1. Such nearly linear dependence on ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} of the fragmentation cross section d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} is indeed observed in the DIPHOX calculation, as reviewed in Sec. III. In reality, some spread of the parton radiation in the direction transverse to the photon’s motion is expected. The treatment of kinematics in parton showering programs like PYTHIA results in somewhat different dependence on zz [12] compared to the collinear approximation, hence in a different magnitude of the fragmentation cross section.

In this work we adopt a procedure that reproduces desirable features of the isolated cross sections, while bypassing some of the difficulties summarized above. To simulate experimental isolation, we reject an event if (a) the separation Δ​r\Delta r between the final-state parton and one of the photons is less than Δ​R\Delta R, and (b) ET​5E_{T5} of the parton is larger than ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso}. This condition is applied to the NLO cross section P⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)P(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}), but not to W⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)W(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) and A⁡(Q,QT,y,θ∗)A(Q,Q_{T},y,\theta_{*}), as these correspond to initial-state QCD radiation and are free of the final-state collinear singularity.

This quasi-experimental isolation excludes the singular final-state direct contributions at ET​5>ETi​s​oE_{T5}>E_{T}^{iso} and Δ​r<Δ​R\Delta r<\Delta R (or sγ​5<ET​γ​ET​5​Δ​R2s_{\gamma 5}<E_{T\gamma}E_{T5}\Delta R^{2}). It is effective for QT>ETi​s​oQ_{T}>E_{T}^{iso}, but the collinear direct contributions survive when QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso}. The integrated (but not the differential) fragmentation rate in the region QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso} may be estimated from a calculation with explicit fragmentation functions. In our approach, we do not introduce fragmentation functions, but we apply an auxiliary regulator to the direct q​gqg cross section at QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso} and Δ​r<Δ​R\Delta r<\Delta R. In our numerical study we find that this prescription preserves a continuous differential distribution except for a small finite discontinuity at QT=ETi​s​oQ_{T}=E_{T}^{iso}. It approximately reproduces the integrated q​gqg rate obtained in the DIPHOX calculation at small QTQ_{T}, for the nominal ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso}.

Two forms of the auxiliary regulator are considered below, based on subtraction of the leading collinear contribution and smooth-cone isolation [25]. In the first case, we subtract the leading part Eq. (20) of the direct q​gqg matrix element when ET​5<ETi​s​oE_{T5}<E_{T}^{iso} and Δ​r<Δ​R.\Delta r<\Delta R. We take z=1−ps⋅p5/(ps⋅pf+ps⋅p5+pf⋅p5),z=1-p_{s}\cdot p_{5}/(p_{s}\cdot p_{f}+p_{s}\cdot p_{5}+p_{f}\cdot p_{5}), where pfμ,p_{f}^{\mu}, p5μ,p_{5}^{\mu}, and psμp_{s}^{\mu} are the four-momenta of the fragmentation photon, fragmentation quark, and spectator photon, respectively [26]. This prescription is used in most of the numerical results in this paper.

In the second case, we suppress fragmentation contributions at Δ​r<Δ​R\Delta r<\Delta R and ET​5<ETi​s​oE_{T5}<E_{T}^{iso} by rejecting events in the Δ​R\Delta R cone that satisfy ET​5<χ⁡(Δ​r)E_{T5}<\chi(\Delta r), where χ⁡(Δ​r)\chi(\Delta r) is a smooth function satisfying χ⁡(0)=0,\chi(0)=0, χ⁡(Δ​R)=ETi​s​o\chi(\Delta R)=E_{T}^{iso}. This “smooth-cone isolation” [25] transforms the fragmentation singularity associated with Dγ​(z,μ)D_{\gamma}(z,\mu) into an integrable singularity, which depends on the assumed functional form of χ⁡(Δ​r)\chi(\Delta r). The cross section for direct contributions is rendered finite by this prescription without explicit introduction of fragmentation functions Dγ​(z,μ)D_{\gamma}(z,\mu). For our smooth function, we choose χ⁡(Δ​r)=ETi​s​o​(1−cos⁡Δ​r)2/(1−cos⁡Δ​R)2\chi(\Delta r)=E_{T}^{iso}(1-\cos\Delta r)^{2}/(1-\cos\Delta R)^{2}, which differs from the specific form considered in Ref. [25], but still satisfies the condition χ⁡(0)=0.\chi(0)=0. Our earlier results in Ref. [2] are computed with this prescription. Here we employ it only in a few instances for comparison with the subtraction method and obtain similar results.

Differences between the two prescriptions can be used to quantify sensitivity of the predictions to the treatment of the QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso} and Δ​r<Δ​R\Delta r<\Delta R region. The two prescriptions yield identical predictions outside of this restricted region, notably at QT>ETi​s​oQ_{T}>E_{T}^{iso}, where our NLO perturbative expression P⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)P(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) in the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg channel is controlled only by quasi-experimental isolation and coincides with the corresponding direct cross section in DIPHOX. The default subtraction prescription predicts a vanishing d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} in the extreme QT→0Q_{T}\rightarrow 0 limit, while the smooth-cone prescription has an integrable singularity in this limit, avoided by an explicit small-QTQ_{T} cutoff in the calculation of our YY-piece. Both prescriptions are free of the logarithmic singularity at QT=ETi​s​oQ_{T}=E_{T}^{iso} arising in the fixed-order (DIPHOX) calculation.

II.3.2 Low-QQ diphoton fragmentation

Another class of large radiative corrections arises when the γ​γ\gamma\gamma invariant mass QQ is smaller than the γ​γ\gamma\gamma transverse momentum QTQ_{T}. In this case, one final-state quark or gluon fragments into a low-mass γ​γ\gamma\gamma pair, e.g. as q+g→(q⟶f​r​a​gγ​γ)+gq+g\rightarrow(q\stackrel{{\scriptstyle frag}}{{\longrightarrow}}\gamma\gamma)+g. The lowest-order contributions of this kind are shown in Fig. 2. The process is described by a γ​γ\gamma\gamma-fragmentation function Dγ​γ​(z1,z2,μ)D_{\gamma\gamma}(z_{1},z_{2},\mu), different from the single-photon fragmentation function Dγ​(z,μ)D_{\gamma}(z,\mu). This new “two-photons from one-fragmentation” contribution is not included yet in existing calculations, even though similar fragmentation mechanisms have been studied in large-QTQ_{T} Drell-Yan pair production [27, 28]. The importance of low-QQ γ​γ\gamma\gamma-fragmentation may be elevated in some kinematic regions for typical experimental cuts. They can be removed by adjustments in the experimental cuts, as discussed in Sec. III.

II.4 Summary of the calculation

We conclude this section by summarizing the main features of our calculation. Full direct NLO cross sections, represented by the graphs (a)-(e), (h)-(l) in Fig. 1, are computed, and their initial-state soft/collinear logarithmic singularities are resummed at small QTQ_{T} in both the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg and g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channels. The perturbative Sudakov functions 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ{\mathcal{B}} and Wilson coefficient functions 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} in the resummed cross section WW are computed up to orders αs3,\alpha_{s}^{3}, αs2\alpha_{s}^{2}, and αs\alpha_{s}, respectively, corresponding to resummation at NNLL accuracy.

Our resummation calculation requires an integration over all values of impact parameter bb, including the nonperturbative region of large bb. In our default calculation of the resummed cross section, we adopt the nonperturbative functions introduced in Ref. [18]. We consider two resummation schemes, the traditional scheme introduced in the CSS paper as well as an alternative scheme [21]. The comparison allows us to estimate the magnitude of yet higher-order corrections that are not included. The size of these effects is different in the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg and g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channels but not particularly significant in either [3].

The final-state collinear singularity in the q​gqg scattering channel is avoided by applying quasi-experimental isolation when QT>ETi​s​oQ_{T}>E_{T}^{iso} and an auxiliary regulator when QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso} to approximate on average the full NLO rate from direct q​gqg and fragmentation cross sections in this QTQ_{T} range. Two prescriptions for the auxiliary regulator (subtraction and smooth isolation inside the photon’s isolation cone) are considered and lead to similar predictions at the Tevatron and LHC.

The singular logarithmic contributions associated with initial-state radiation are subtracted from the NLO cross section PP to form a regular piece Y,Y, which is added to the small-QTQ_{T} resummed cross section WW to predict the production rate for small and intermediate values of QTQ_{T}. In the g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channel, we also subtract from PP a new singular spin-flip contribution that affects azimuthal angle (OPENφ∗)\varphi_{*}) dependence in the Collins-Soper reference frame. We switch our prediction to the fixed-order perturbative result PP at the point in QTQ_{T} where the cross section W+YW+Y drops below PP. This crossing point is located at QTQ_{T} of order QQ in both q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg and g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channels.

III Comparisons with Data and Predictions

Our calculation of the differential cross section d​σ/(d​Q​d​QT​d​y​d​Ω∗)d\sigma/(dQdQ_{T}dyd\Omega_{*}) is especially pertinent for the transverse momentum QTQ_{T} distribution in the region QT≲QQ_{T}\lesssim Q, for fixed values of diphoton mass QQ (cf. Section III.1.1). It would be best to compare our multiple differential distribution with experiment, but published collider data tend to be presented in the form of singly differential distributions in QQ, QTQ_{T}, and Δ​φ≡φ3−φ4\Delta\varphi\equiv\varphi_{3}-\varphi_{4} in the lab frame, after integration over the other independent kinematic variables. We follow suit in order to make comparisons with Tevatron collider data, but we recommend that more differential studies be made, and we comment on the features that can be explored. We show results at the energy of the Tevatron collider and then make predictions for the Large Hadron Collider.

The analytical results of Sec. II are implemented in our computer code. As a first step, resummed and NLO γ​γ\gamma\gamma cross sections are computed on a grid of discrete values of QQ, QTQ_{T}, and yy by using the resummation program Legacy described in Refs. [29, 30]. At the second stage, matching of the resummed and NLO cross sections is performed, and fully differential cross sections are evaluated by Monte-Carlo integration of the matched grids in the latest version of the program ResBos [31, 32]. The calculation is done for Nf=5N_{f}=5 active quark flavors and the following values of the electroweak and strong interaction parameters [33]:

GF=1.16639×10−5​GeV−2,mZ=91.1882​GeV,\displaystyle G_{F}=1.16639\times 10^{-5}\penalty\ \textrm{GeV}^{-2},\penalty\ \penalty\ m_{Z}=91.1882\penalty\ {\textrm{GeV}}, (21)
α⁡(mZ)=1/128.937,αs​(mZ)=0.1187.\displaystyle\alpha(m_{Z})=1/128.937,\penalty\ \penalty\ \alpha_{s}(m_{Z})=0.1187. (22)

The following choices of the factorization constants are used: C1=C3=2​e−γE≈1.123​…C_{1}=C_{3}=2e^{-\gamma_{E}}\approx 1.123..., and C2=C4=1.C_{2}=C_{4}=1. The choice C4=1C_{4}=1 implies that we equate the renormalization and factorization scales to the invariant mass of the photon pair, μR=μF=Q\mu_{R}=\mu_{F}=Q, in the fixed-order and asymptotic contributions P⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)P(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) and A⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)A(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}). We use two-loop expressions for the running electromagnetic and strong couplings α⁡(μ)\alpha(\mu) and αS​(μ)\alpha_{S}(\mu), as well as the NLO parton distribution function set CTEQ6M [19] with Qi​n​i=1.3Q_{ini}=1.3 GeV. For calculations with explicit final-state fragmentation functions included, we use set 1 of the NLO photon fragmentation functions from Ref. [34].

III.1 Results for Run 2 at the Tevatron

III.1.1 Kinematic constraints

In this section, we present our results for the Tevatron p​p¯p\bar{p} collider operating at S=1.96\sqrt{S}=1.96 TeV. In order to compare with the data from the Collider Detector at Fermilab (CDF) collaboration [1], we make the same restrictions on the final-state photons as those used in the experimental measurement (unless stated otherwise):

transverse momentum​pTγ>pT​m​i​nγ=14​(13)​GeV for the harder (softer) photon,\displaystyle{\textrm{transverse momentum}}\penalty\ p_{T}^{\gamma}>p_{T\,min}^{\gamma}=14\penalty\ (13)\penalty\ {\textrm{GeV for the harder (softer) photon, }} (23)
and rapidity​|yγ|<0.9​for each photon.\displaystyle{\textrm{and rapidity}}\penalty\ |y^{\gamma}|<0.9\penalty\ {\textrm{for each photon}}. (24)

We impose isolation conditions described in Section II.3, assuming the nominal isolation energy ETi​s​o=1E_{T}^{iso}=1 GeV specified in the CDF publication, along with Δ​R=0.4,\Delta R=0.4, and Δ​Rγ​γ=0.3\Delta R_{\gamma\gamma}=0.3.

We also show predictions for the constraints that approximate event selection conditions used by the Fermilab DØ Collaboration [35]: pTγ>pT​m​i​nγ=21​(20)p_{T}^{\gamma}>p_{T\,min}^{\gamma}=21\penalty\ (20) GeV for the harder (softer) photon, |yγ|<1.1|y^{\gamma}|<1.1, and ETi​s​o/ETγ=0.07E_{T}^{iso}/E_{T}^{\gamma}=0.07 for each photon, for the same Δ​R\Delta R and Δ​Rγ​γ\Delta R_{\gamma\gamma} values as in the CDF case.

A scatter plot of event distributions from our theoretical simulation for CDF kinematic cuts and arbitrary luminosity is shown in Fig. 3. The events are plotted versus the invariant mass QQ, transverse momentum QTQ_{T}, rapidity separation |Δ​y|≡|yh​a​r​d−ys​o​f​t|\left|\Delta y\right|\equiv\left|y_{hard}-y_{soft}\right|, and azimuthal separation Δ​φ≡|φh​a​r​d−φs​o​f​t|\Delta\varphi\equiv\left|\varphi_{hard}-\varphi_{soft}\right| (with OPEN0≤Δ​φ≤π)0\leq\Delta\varphi\leq\pi) between the harder and softer photon in the lab frame, as well as the cosine of the polar angle θ∗\theta_{*} in the Collins-Soper frame. It can be seen from the figure that Δ​φ\Delta\varphi is correlated with the difference QT−QQ_{T}-Q. Events with QT<QQ_{T}<Q (QT>QQ_{T}>Q) tend to populate regions with Δ​φ>π/2\Delta\varphi>\pi/2 (Δ​φ<π/2\Delta\varphi<\pi/2). The extreme case QT=0Q_{T}=0 relevant to the Born approximation corresponds to Δ​φ=π\Delta\varphi=\pi.

The pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} cuts suppress the mass region Q≲2​pT​m​i​nγ3​pT​m​i​nγ4≈27Q\lesssim 2\sqrt{p_{Tmin}^{\gamma_{3}}p_{Tmin}^{\gamma_{4}}}\approx 27 GeV at Δ​φ≈π\Delta\varphi\approx\pi and QT≲25Q_{T}\lesssim 25 GeV at Δ​φ≈0\Delta\varphi\approx 0, leading to the appearance of a kinematic cutoff in the invariant mass distribution and a “shoulder” in the transverse momentum distribution, as shown in later sections. Our theoretical framework is applicable in the region QT≲QQ_{T}\lesssim Q (large Δ​φ\Delta\varphi), where the dominant fraction of events occurs. The appearance of singularities in the NLO calculation at QT→0Q_{T}\rightarrow 0 and the fact that there are two different hard scales, QTQ_{T} and QQ, relevant for the event distributions in the low-QTQ_{T} region require that we address and resum large logarithmic terms of the form log⁡(Q/QT)\log(Q/Q_{T}). Different and interesting physics becomes important in the complementary region QT>QQ_{T}>Q (small Δ​φ\Delta\varphi), a topic we address in Sec. III.1.3.

III.1.2 Tevatron cross sections

We compare our resummed and finite-order predictions for the invariant mass (QQ) distribution of photon pairs, shown in Fig. 4 as solid and dashed lines, respectively. The finite-order cross section is evaluated at O⁡(αs)O(\alpha_{s}) accuracy in the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg channel and at O⁡(αs3)O(\alpha_{s}^{3}) accuracy in the g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channel. These finite-order calculations are performed with the phase-space slicing method described in Sec. II.2. When integrated over all QTQ_{T}, as in the d​σ/d​Qd\sigma/dQ distribution at large QQ, the resummed logarithmic terms from higher orders in αs\alpha_{s} produce a relatively small NNLO correction, such that the resummed and finite-order mass distributions in Fig. 4 are close to one another in normalization and shape. Both distributions also agree with the CDF data in this QQ range within experimental uncertainties.

The shape of d​σ/d​Qd\sigma/dQ at small QQ is affected by the cuts in Eq. (23) on the transverse momenta pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} of the two photons. In addition to being responsible for the characteristic cutoff at Q≈27Q\approx 27 GeV explained in the previous subsection, the cuts on the individual transverse momenta pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} also introduce a dependence of the invariant mass distribution on the shape of the QTQ_{T} spectrum of the γ​γ\gamma\gamma pairs. Because of this correlation between the QQ and QTQ_{T} distributions, the discontinuities in d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} as QT→0Q_{T}\rightarrow 0, when computed at finite order, make finite-order predictions for d​σ/d​Qd\sigma/dQ somewhat unstable.

The finite-order expectation for the transverse momentum distribution d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} (i.e., the integral of P⁡(Q,QT,y,Ω∗)P(Q,Q_{T},y,\Omega_{*}) over QQ, yy, and Ω∗\Omega_{*}, or PP for brevity) is shown as a dashed curve in Fig. 5(a). It exhibits an integrable singularity in the small-QTQ_{T} limit. Terms with inverse power and logarithmic dependence on QTQ_{T}, associated with initial-state radiation as QT→0Q_{T}\rightarrow 0, are extracted from PP and form the asymptotic contribution, denoted as AA (dotted curve). In the figure, both PP and AA are truncated at a small value of QTQ_{T}, that is, not drawn all the way to QT=0Q_{T}=0. The curves for PP and AA are close at small values of QTQ_{T}, signaling that the initial-state logarithmic singularities dominate the NLO distribution. The difference YY between the PP and AA distributions includes the finite regular terms not included in AA and logarithmic terms from the final-state fragmentation singularities, with the latter subtracted when QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso}, as described in Sec. II.3. The data clearly disfavor the fixed-order prediction in the region of low QTQ_{T}.

Figure 5(b) features the resummed W+YW+Y contribution (solid curve). Resummation of the initial-state logarithmic terms renders WW finite in the region of small QTQ_{T}. The sum of WW and YY includes the resummed initial-state singular contributions plus the remaining relevant terms in PP. Since PP provides a reliable fixed-order estimate at large QTQ_{T}, we present our final resummed prediction by switching from W+YW+Y to PP at the point at which the two differential cross sections (as functions of QQ, QTQ_{T} and yy) cross each other. In contrast to the fixed-order (dashed) curve PP in Fig. 5(b), the agreement with data is improved at the lowest values of QTQ_{T}, where resummation brings the rate down, and for QT=12−32Q_{T}=12-32 GeV, where the resummed logarithmic terms increase the rate.

The resummed predictions for the Tevatron experiments are practically insensitive to the choice of the resummation scheme and the nonperturbative model [3]. About 75% (25%) of the total rate at the Tevatron with CDF cuts imposed comes from the q​q¯+q​g+q¯​gq{\bar{q}}+qg+{\bar{q}}g (g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S}) initial state. The fractions for the cuts used by DØ are 84% and 16%. The g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} contribution falls steeply after QT>22Q_{T}>22 GeV, because the gluon PDF decreases rapidly with parton fractional momentum xx [3].

The distribution in the difference Δ​φ\Delta\varphi of the azimuthal angles of the photons is shown in Fig. 6. As is true for the transverse momentum distribution in the limit QT→0Q_{T}\rightarrow 0, the distribution computed at fixed order is ill-defined at Δ​φ=π\Delta\varphi=\pi. The resummed distribution shows a larger cross section near Δ​φ=2.5\Delta\varphi=2.5 rad, in better agreement with the data. In the region of small Δ​φ≲π/2\Delta\varphi\lesssim\pi/2, the fixed-order and the resummed predictions are the same, a result of our matching of the resummed and fixed-order distributions at mid to high values of QTQ_{T}. Although the cross section is not large in the region Δ​φ<π/2\Delta\varphi<\pi/2, there is an indication of a difference between our predictions and data in this region, a topic we address below.

III.1.3 The region QT>QQ_{T}>Q

It is evident from Fig. 3 that the Δ​φ<π/2\Delta\varphi<\pi/2 region is populated mostly by events with QT>QQ_{T}>Q. New types of radiative contributions may be present in this region, including various fragmentation contributions described in Sec. II.3 and enhancements at large |cos⁡θ∗||\cos\theta_{*}| in the direct production rate.

While experimental isolation generally suppresses long-distance fragmentation, a greater fraction of fragmentation photons are expected to survive isolation when Δ​φ<π/2\Delta\varphi<\pi/2. Besides single-photon ‘one-fragmentation’ and ‘two-fragmentation’ contributions (with one photon per fragmenting parton), one encounters additional logarithmic singularities of the form log⁡(Q/QT)\log(Q/Q_{T}). We noted in Sec. II.3 that these logarithms are associated with the fragmentation of a parton carrying large transverse momentum QTQ_{T} into a system of small invariant mass QQ [27, 28], a light γ​γ\gamma\gamma pair in our case. Small-QQ γ​γ\gamma\gamma fragmentation of this kind is not implemented yet in theoretical models. Therefore, we are prepared for the possibility that both the fixed-order calculation and our resummed calculation may be deficient in the region QT≫QQ_{T}\gg Q. A detailed experimental study of the region QT>QQ_{T}>Q may offer the opportunity to measure the parton to two-photon fragmentation function Dγ​γ​(z1,z2)D_{\gamma\gamma}(z_{1},z_{2}), provided that the single-photon ‘one-fragmentation’ function Dγ​(z)D_{\gamma}(z) is determined by single-photon data, and the low-QQ logarithmic terms are properly resummed theoretically.

In addition to the low-QQ fragmentation, the small-Δ​φ\Delta\varphi region may be sensitive to large higher-order contributions associated with t^\widehat{t}- or u^\widehat{u}-channel exchanges in the q​q¯→γ​γq\bar{q}\rightarrow\gamma\gamma and g​g→γ​γgg\rightarrow\gamma\gamma subprocesses. In the Born processes in Figs. 1(a) and (h), the t^\widehat{t}- and u^\widehat{u}-channel singularities arise at cos⁡θ∗≈±1\cos\theta_{*}\approx\pm 1 and Δ​φ≈π\Delta\varphi\approx\pi. These singularities are excluded by the pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} cuts in Eq. (23), but related residual enhancements in the NLO contributions may still persist at |cos⁡θ∗|≈1|\cos\theta_{*}|\approx 1 and Δ​φ→0\Delta\varphi\rightarrow 0, not excluded by the cuts (cf. Fig. 3). Because |cos⁡θ∗|\left|\cos\theta_{*}\right| is large in such events, they tend to have substantial |Δ​y||\Delta y|, so they are retained by the Δ​Rγ​γ>0.3\Delta R_{\gamma\gamma}>0.3 cut. In contrast, the low-QQ fragmentation contributions tend to be abundant at small |Δ​y||\Delta y|. It may be therefore possible to distinguish between the large-|cos⁡θ∗||\cos\theta_{*}| and fragmentation events at small Δ​φ\Delta\varphi based on the distribution in |Δ​y||\Delta y|.

We expect much better agreement of our predictions with data if the selection QT<QQ_{T}<Q is made. This selection preserves the bulk of the cross section and assures that a fair comparison is made in the region of phase space where the predictions are most valid.

III.1.4 Fragmentation and comparison with the DIPHOX code

One way to obtain an estimate of theoretical uncertainty is to compare theoretical approaches in various parts of phase space, including small Δ​φ\Delta\varphi. We handle the collinear final-state photon singularities in the manner described in Sec. II, without including photon fragmentation functions explicitly. An alternative calculation implemented in the DIPHOX code [14] includes NLO cross sections for single-photon fragmentation processes. Neither code includes a term in which both photons are fragmentation products of the same final-state parton, i.e., the diphoton fragmentation function Dγ​γ​(z1,z2)D_{\gamma\gamma}(z_{1},z_{2}).

In Ref. [2] we show comparisons of our predictions with those of DIPHOX along with the CDF data. Here in Fig. 7, we show analogous plots of the invariant mass and transverse momentum distributions for DØ cuts. We note that our fixed-order q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg contribution agrees well with the direct contribution in DIPHOX. This agreement is particularly impressive in the region of large QTQ_{T}, where both codes use the same fixed-order formalism to handle direct contributions. A contribution from the g​ggg channel is also present in both codes, computed at LO in DIPHOX but at NLO+NNLL in our case. Since the g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} contribution is not dominant (especially in the high QTQ_{T} region), this difference does not have a significant impact on the comparison.

The explicit single-photon fragmentation contributions in DIPHOX (mostly ‘one-fragmentation’ contribution) are quite small for the nominal hadronic energy ETi​s​o∼1E_{T}^{iso}\sim 1 GeV in the cone around each photon. Exceptions occur in the region QT≤ETi​s​oQ_{T}\leq E_{T}^{iso}, where the fragmentation contributions to d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} have logarithmic singularities, and in the Δ​φ→0\Delta\varphi\rightarrow 0 region, where fragmentation is comparable to the direct contributions. Our isolation prescription reproduces the integrated DIPHOX rate well for 0≤QT≤ETi​s​o0\leq Q_{T}\leq E_{T}^{iso}, leading to close agreement between the resummed and DIPHOX inclusive rates for most QQ values.

Returning to the CDF measurement, we remark that the resummed and DIPHOX cross sections for the same ETi​s​o=1E_{T}^{iso}=1 GeV underestimate the data within two standard deviations for Q≲27Q\lesssim 27 GeV, QT>25Q_{T}>25 GeV, and Δ​φ<1\Delta\varphi<1 rad (cf. the relevant figures in Ref. [2]). The DIPHOX cross section can be raised to agree with data in this “shoulder” region, if a much larger isolation energy (ETi​s​o=4E_{T}^{iso}=4 GeV) is chosen, and smaller factorization and renormalization scales are used (μF=μR=Q/2\mu_{F}=\mu_{R}=Q/2). These are the choices made in the CDF study [1]. Since ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} is an approximate characteristic of the experimental isolation, one might argue that both ETi​s​o=1E_{T}^{iso}=1 and 4 GeV can be appropriate in a calculation to match the conditions of the CDF measurement. The direct contribution is weakly sensitive to ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso}, while the one-fragmentation part of d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} is roughly proportional to ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} (cf. Section II.3). The one-fragmentation contribution is enhanced on average by 400% if ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} is increased in the calculation from 1 to 4 GeV. The rate in the shoulder region is enhanced further if the factorization scale μF\mu_{F} is reduced.

Since the theoretical specifications for isolation and for the fragmentation contribution are admittedly approximate, we question whether great importance should be placed on the agreement of theory and experiment in the region of small Δ​φ\Delta\varphi or in the shoulder region in the QTQ_{T} distribution. A straightforward way to reduce sensitivity to fragmentation is to require Q>27Q>27 GeV or QT<QQ_{T}<Q, as discussed above. The two cuts have similar effects on the event distributions. Figure 8 shows the effects of the QT<QQ_{T}<Q cut on the QTQ_{T} and Δ​φ\Delta\varphi distributions. The cut QT<QQ_{T}<Q is particularly efficient at suppressing the fragmentation QTQ_{T} shoulder (and the region of small Δ​φ\Delta\varphi altogether), while only a small portion of the event sample is lost. This cut is especially favorable, since it constrains the comparison with data to a region where the theory is well understood and has a small uncertainty. Furthermore, with the requirement of QT<QQ_{T}<Q, the dependence of differential cross sections on the choices of isolation energy ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} and factorization scale μF\mu_{F} is greatly reduced to the typical size of higher-order corrections. We predict that if a QT<QQ_{T}<Q cut, or a Q>27Q>27 GeV cut, is applied to the Tevatron data, the enhancement at low Δ​φ\Delta\varphi and intermediate QTQ_{T} associated with the fragmentation contribution will disappear. This is an important conclusion of our study, and we urge the CDF and DØ  collaborations to apply these cuts in their future analyses of the diphoton data.

III.1.5 Average transverse momentum

An important prediction of the resummation formalism is the change of the transverse momentum distribution with the diphoton invariant mass. This dependence comes, in part, from the ln⁡Q2\ln Q^{2} dependence in the Sudakov exponent, Eq. (17), and it is desirable to identify this feature amid other influences. In Fig. 9(a), we show normalized resummed transverse momentum distributions for various selections of the invariant mass of the photon pairs. Without kinematical constraints on the decay photons, the QTQ_{T} distribution is expected to broaden with increasing QQ, and the position of the peak in d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} to shift to larger QTQ_{T} values. The shift of the peak may or may not be observed in the data depending on the chosen lower cuts on pTp_{T} of the photons, which suppress the event rate at low QQ and QTQ_{T}. The interplay of the Sudakov broadening of the QTQ_{T} distribution and kinematical suppression by the photon pTp_{T} cuts is reflected in the shape of d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} in different QQ bins.

According to dimensional analysis, the average ⟨QT⟩\langle Q_{T}\rangle in the interval QT≤QQ_{T}\leq Q may be expected to behave as

⟨QT⟩QT≤Q=Q​f​(Q/S),\langle Q_{T}\rangle_{Q_{T}\leq Q}=Qf(Q/\sqrt{S}), (25)

where the scaling function f⁡(Q/SCLOSEf(Q/\sqrt{S}) reflects phase space constraints, dependence on the Sudakov logarithm, and the xx dependence of the PDFs. Figure 9(b) shows our calculated diphoton mass dependence of ⟨QT⟩\langle Q_{T}\rangle. The linear increase shown in Eq. (25) is observed over the range 30<Q<8030<Q<80 GeV. For values of QQ below the kinematic cutoff at about 30 GeV, the cuts shown in Fig. 3 suppress diphoton production at small QTQ_{T}, and ⟨QT/Q⟩\langle Q_{T}/Q\rangle grows toward 1 as QQ decreases (corresponding to production only at QTQ_{T} close to QQ). For Q∼80Q\sim 80 GeV and above, we see a saturation of the growth of ⟨QT⟩\langle Q_{T}\rangle, a reflection of the influences of the xx dependence of the PDFs and other factors. Similar saturation behavior is observed in calculations of ⟨QT⟩\langle Q_{T}\rangle in other processes [36]. It would be interesting to see a comparison of our prediction with data from the CDF and DØ collaborations.

III.2 Results for the LHC

III.2.1 Event selection

To obtain predictions for p​ppp collisions at the LHC at S=14\sqrt{S}=14 TeV, we employ the cuts on the individual photons used by the ATLAS collaboration in their simulations of Higgs boson decay, h→γ​γh\rightarrow\gamma\gamma [37]. We require

transverse momentum​pTγ>40​(25)​GeV for the harder (softer) photon,\displaystyle{\textrm{transverse momentum}}\penalty\ p_{T}^{\gamma}>40\penalty\ (25)\penalty\ {\textrm{GeV for the harder (softer) photon, }} (26)
and rapidity​|yγ|<2.5​for each photon.\displaystyle{\textrm{and rapidity}}\penalty\ |y^{\gamma}|<2.5\penalty\ {\textrm{for each photon}}. (27)

In accord with ATLAS specifications, we impose a looser isolation restriction than for our Tevatron study, requiring less than ETi​s​o=15E_{T}^{iso}=15 GeV of hadronic and extra electromagnetic transverse energy inside a Δ​R=0.4\Delta R=0.4 cone around each photon. We also require the separation Δ​Rγ​γ\Delta R_{\gamma\gamma} between the two isolated photons to be above 0.4.

The cuts listed above, optimized for the Higgs boson search, may require adjustments in order to test perturbative QCD predictions in the full γ​γ\gamma\gamma invariant mass range accessible at the LHC. The values of the pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} cuts on the photons in Eq. (26) preserve a large fraction of Higgs boson events with Q>115Q>115 GeV. These cuts may be too restrictive in studies of γ​γ\gamma\gamma production at smaller QQ, considering that the two final-state photons most likely originate from a γ​γ\gamma\gamma pair with small QTQ_{T} and have similar values of pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} of about Q/2Q/2. The pTp_{T} cuts interfere with the expected Sudakov broadening of QTQ_{T} distributions with increasing diphoton invariant mass, as discussed in Section III.1.5. We further note that the asymmetry between the pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} cuts on the harder and softer photons is necessary in a fixed-order perturbative QCD calculation, but it is not required in the resummed calculation. At a fixed order of αs\alpha_{s}, asymmetry in the pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} cuts prevents instabilities in d​σ/d​Qd\sigma/dQ caused by logarithmic divergences in d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} at small QTQ_{T}. Such instabilities are eliminated altogether once the small-QTQ_{T} logarithmic terms are resummed to all orders of αs\alpha_{s}. Here we do not consider alternative pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} cuts, although experimental collaborations are encouraged to employ relaxed and/or symmetric cuts to increase the γ​γ\gamma\gamma event sample in their data analysis.

III.2.2 Resummed QTQ_{T} distributions and average transverse momentum

Figure 10 shows transverse momentum distributions of the photon pairs for various invariant masses. The average γ​γ\gamma\gamma transverse momentum grows with QQ, as demonstrated by Fig. 11. However, the rate of the growth decreases monotonically with Q,Q, for similar reasons as at the Tevatron.

The γ​γ\gamma\gamma distributions in QQ and Δ​φ\Delta\varphi for different combinations of scattering subchannels and choices of theoretical parameters are discussed in Refs. [2, 3]. In all ranges of QQ, the γ​γ\gamma\gamma production rate is dominated by a large q​gqg contribution, accounting for about 50% of the fixed-order (NLO) rate. Although this number depends on the choice of the factorization scheme and scale, and, on the other hand, separate treatment of the q​q¯q\bar{q} and q​gqg cross sections is not meaningful in the resummation calculation [3], it nonetheless reflects, in a crude way, the increased relative importance of the q​gqg cross section. The g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channel contributes about 25% at Q∼80Q\sim 80 GeV (the location of the cutoff in d​σ/d​Qd\sigma/dQ due to the cuts on pTγp_{T}^{\gamma}) and less at larger Q.Q. As at the Tevatron, the dependence of the cross sections on the resummation scheme is small [3]. The dependence on the nonperturbative model can also be neglected, as long as the nonperturbative function does not vary strongly with xx [3].

III.2.3 Final-state fragmentation and comparison with DIPHOX

The impact of the final-state fragmentation at the LHC can be evaluated if we compare our results with DIPHOX predictions. The transverse momentum and invariant mass distributions in the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg channel from the two approaches are shown in Fig. 12. In both calculations, quasi-experimental isolation removes direct NLO events with collinear final-state photons and partons when QT>ETi​s​o=15Q_{T}>E_{T}^{iso}=15 GeV, but not when QTQ_{T} is below ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso}.

Concentrating first on γ​γ\gamma\gamma events with QT>ETi​s​oQ_{T}>E_{T}^{iso}, we observe that, at QT>80Q_{T}>80 GeV, the resummed q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg cross section reduces to the direct fixed-order cross section, evaluated in the same way as in the DIPHOX code. Our resummed and the direct DIPHOX cross sections, shown as solid and dashed curves, respectively, in Fig. 12(a) consequently agree well at large QTQ_{T}. At smaller QT,Q_{T}, the resummed cross section is enhanced by towers of higher-order logarithmic contributions. On the other hand, the full q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg DIPHOX rate (shown as a dotted line) also includes single-photon fragmentation contributions, which add to the direct production cross section. For the nominal isolation parameters, the explicit fragmentation contribution constitutes about 25% of the full DIPHOX rate for 60<QT<12060<Q_{T}<120 GeV. Its magnitude increases approximately linearly with the assumed ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} value.

For QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso}, the final-state collinear region of the direct contribution is regulated by the collinear subtraction prescription adopted in the resummation calculation, whereas the fragmentation singularity is subtracted from the direct contribution and replaced by photon fragmentation functions in the DIPHOX calculation. Subtraction of singularities in DIPHOX introduces integrable singularities in d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} at different values of QTQ_{T} below ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso}. The origin of the final-state logarithmic singularities at values of QTQ_{T} below ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} is discussed in Refs. [22, 23, 24]. For QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso}, the DIPHOX curves represent the average over singular contributions in this QTQ_{T} interval.

After the fragmentation singularity is subtracted, the DIPHOX direct contribution (dashed line) is on average below our resummed q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg rate (solid line) over most of the range of QTQ_{T} shown in Fig. 12(a). After integration over all QTQ_{T}, our resummed and DIPHOX q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg cross sections agree within 10-20% at most values of QQ (cf. Fig. 12(b)), with our resummed rate being below the DIPHOX rate at all QQ. The largest difference occurs at the lowest values of QQ (below the cutoff), where the rates can differ by a factor of 2. In this region, corresponding to diphoton events with small Δ​φ\Delta\varphi and QTQ_{T} larger than QQ, the photon fragmentation contributions included in the DIPHOX calculation are large in comparison to the direct rate. Finally, we note that the integrated rate in DIPHOX is more stable with respect to variations in ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} than the differential distributions in DIPHOX, because ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} dependence for QT>ETi​s​oQ_{T}>E_{T}^{iso} is canceled to a good degree by ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} dependence for QT<ETi​s​o.Q_{T}<E_{T}^{iso}.

To obtain the final γ​γ\gamma\gamma production cross sections, after inclusion of all channels, we combine the respective q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg results with the resummed NLO g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} cross section in our case and with the LO g​ggg cross section in the DIPHOX case. The distributions in the γ​γ\gamma\gamma invariant mass Q,Q, the transverse momentum QTQ_{T}, and the azimuthal angle separation Δ​φ\Delta\varphi in the lab frame are shown in Fig. 13. For the cuts chosen, the LO g​ggg and the resummed g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} total rates constitute about 9% and 20% of the total rate. The resummed and DIPHOX invariant mass distributions (Fig. 13(a)) are brought closer to one another as a result of the inclusion of the g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} contribution in the resummed calculation. For QT≠0Q_{T}\neq 0, the full DIPHOX QTQ_{T} distribution in Fig. 13(b) is determined entirely by direct plus fragmentation contributions (the same as in Fig. 12(a)), because the LO g​ggg cross section contributes at QT=0Q_{T}=0 only. In contrast, our resummed g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} contribution modifies the event rate at all QTQ_{T}.

The resummed and DIPHOX rates are in a reasonable agreement for 1.5≲Δ​φ≲2.51.5\lesssim\Delta\varphi\lesssim 2.5, as shown in Fig. 13(c). In the Δ​φ→π\Delta\varphi\rightarrow\pi limit, the fixed-order rates in DIPHOX diverge because of the singularities at small QTQ_{T}, while our resummed rate yields a finite value. For Δ​φ<1.5\Delta\varphi<1.5, the DIPHOX cross section is enhanced by photon fragmentation contributions. As at the energy of the Tevatron, theoretical uncertainties are greater at small Δ​φ\Delta\varphi.

Predictions are most reliable when QT<QQ_{T}<Q (and the angles θ∗\theta_{*} and φ∗\varphi_{*} are away from 0 or π\pi). With the QT<QQ_{T}<Q cut imposed, the uncertain large-QTQ_{T} photon fragmentation contributions are suppressed, and the resummed and DIPHOX cross sections agree well at large QTQ_{T} (cf. Fig. 14(b)). The QTQ_{T} distribution in the interval 70<Q<11570<Q<115 GeV with the QT<QQ_{T}<Q constraint is shown in Fig. 10 by a dotted curve. Distributions in the other two mass bins in Fig. 10 are essentially not affected by this cut in the QTQ_{T} range presented.

Our calculation captures the dominant contributions to γ​γ\gamma\gamma production at the LHC. However, as we noted, direct q​gqg scattering, evaluated at order 𝒪⁡(αs){\mathcal{O}}(\alpha_{s}) in our calculation, is the leading scattering channel in the region relevant for the Higgs boson search at the LHC. It is important to emphasize that the final-state collinear radiation is not the main reason behind the enhancement of the q​gqg rate, which is increased predominantly by contributions from non-singular phase space regions. Consequently, the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg direct rate is only weakly sensitive to adjustments in the isolation parameters ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} and Δ​R\Delta R [10]. The unknown 𝒪⁡(αs2){\mathcal{O}}(\alpha_{s}^{2}) contributions to q​gqg scattering may be non-negligible, and it would be valuable to compute them in the future when LHC data are available.

III.3 Comparison with Higgs boson signal distributions

We highlight some similarities and differences between the production spectra for the Higgs boson signal and the QCD background discussed in this paper. We focus on the diphoton decay mode of a SM Higgs boson produced from the dominant gluon-fusion mechanism, g​g→h0→γ​γgg\rightarrow h^{0}\rightarrow\gamma\gamma, where the Higgs boson production cross section is calculated at the same order of precision as the QCD continuum background. We include initial-state QCD contributions at O⁡(αs3)O(\alpha_{s}^{3}) (NLO) and resummed contributions at NNLL accuracy. These contributions are also coded in ResBos [38], and we can apply the same cuts on the momenta of the photons to the signal and background. Our findings should remain broadly applicable after the NNLO corrections to Higgs boson production [39, 40] are included. We compute the background in the range 128<Q<132128<Q<132 GeV, and the signal at a fixed Higgs boson mass mH=130m_{H}=130 GeV. We impose the kinematic selection QT<QQ_{T}<Q, but its influence is not important at the large values of diphoton mass of interest here.

The cross section times branching ratio for the Higgs boson signal is substantially smaller than the QCD continuum. To better illustrate their differences, Fig. 15 presents distributions normalized to the respective total rates. The top-left panel shows normalized transverse momentum distributions of photon pairs. The signal and background peak at about 12 and 5 GeV, respectively. The average values of QTQ_{T} are 26 and 23 GeV, computed over the range 0 to 75 GeV.

Differences in the shapes of these QTQ_{T} spectra can be attributed to the different structure of the leading terms in the initial-state Sudakov exponents and to the effects of final-state photon fragmentation. The Higgs boson signal is controlled by the characteristics of the g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} initial state, whereas the continuum is controlled primarily by the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg initial state. Because the dominant Sudakov coefficient 𝒜q(k)∝CF\mathcal{A}_{q}^{(k)}\propto C_{F} in the q​q¯q\bar{q} case is smaller than 𝒜g(k)=(CA/CF)​𝒜q(k)\mathcal{A}_{g}^{(k)}=(C_{A}/C_{F})\mathcal{A}_{q}^{(k)} in the g​ggg case, the resummed q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg initial-state radiation produces narrower QTQ_{T} distributions than g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} initial-state radiation. About 80% of the diphoton rate is provided by the q​q¯+q​gq\bar{q}+qg channel, implying a narrower QTQ_{T} distribution of the background, if based on the value of 𝒜(k)\mathcal{A}^{(k)} alone.

The continuum background contribution is also enhanced by final-state radiation in q​gqg scattering. The QTQ_{T} profile of the final-state collinear terms depends more on the isolation model (including ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} and Δ​R\Delta R) than on the initial-state Sudakov exponent. For the nominal ATLAS cuts, the final-state collinear contribution in our calculation hardens the background QTQ_{T} distribution, diminishing its difference from the Higgs boson signal distribution. More effective isolation may reduce the impact of the final-state radiation on QTQ_{T} distributions.

Another difference between the signal and continuum is observed in the distribution in the azimuthal angle of the photons, such as the angle φ∗\varphi_{*} in the Collins-Soper frame shown in the top-right panel of Fig. 15. This distribution is qualitatively the same if integrated over all QTQ_{T}, as in Fig. 15, or integrated above some minimal QTQ_{T} value, as in an experimental measurement. Without isolation imposed, the spin-00 Higgs boson signal must be flat in φ∗,\varphi_{*}, but the QCD background peaks toward φ∗=0\varphi_{*}=0 and π\pi (i.e., sin⁡φ∗=0\sin\varphi_{*}=0) as a result of the final-state q​gqg singularity.22 2 By definition, the recoil parton 5 always lies in the O​x​zOxz plane (has zero azimuthal angle) in the Collins-Soper frame. For the final-state singularity to occur at NLO, the photons should be in the same plane with 5, i.e., have sin⁡φ∗=0\sin\varphi_{*}=0., 33 3 One of the resummed structure functions for the g​ggg background is modulated by cos⁡2​φ∗\cos 2\varphi_{*} (see Sec. II.2), but we neglect this modulation in our present calculation. Isolation cuts suppress both the signal and the background for sin⁡φ∗<sin⁡Δ​R\sin\varphi_{*}<\sin\Delta R. The result is a signal distribution with a broad peak near φ∗=π/2\varphi_{*}=\pi/2, while the background favors values of φ∗\varphi_{*} near 00 and π\pi. A selection of events with φ∗\varphi_{*} in the vicinity of π/2\pi/2, and QTQ_{T} large enough, helps to reduce the impact of the q​gqg background.In the lab frame, a related distribution is in the variable |φ3​T−φ4​T|,\left|\varphi_{3T}-\varphi_{4T}\right|,where φi​T\varphi_{iT} is the azimuthal angle between p→Tγi\vec{p}_{T}^{\gamma_{i}} and Q→T\vec{Q}_{T}. The signal (background) processes tend to have more events with large (small) magnitude of |φ3​T−φ4​T|\left|\varphi_{3T}-\varphi_{4T}\right|.

A third potential discriminator between the signal and background is the difference in the rapidities Δ​y=yh​a​r​d−ys​o​f​t\Delta y=y_{hard}-y_{soft} of the photons with harder and softer values of pTγp_{T}^{\gamma} in the lab frame, calculated on an event by event basis. This distribution is displayed in the lower-left frame of Fig. 15. The background distribution peaks at the origin, while the signal is almost flat over a wide range of Δ​y\Delta y. Different spin correlations in the decay of a spin-0 Higgs boson from those characteristic of QCD background processes are the source of this distinction. Discrimination based on this difference can improve the statistical significance of the signal [10]. We note that our resummed calculation does not exhibit the kinematic singularity at Δ​y≈2\Delta y\approx 2 present in the finite-order cross section and obvious in Fig. 10 of Ref. [10], where the distribution with respect to y∗≡Δ​y/2y^{*}\equiv\Delta y/2 is shown. The discontinuity in d​σ/d​QTd\sigma/dQ_{T} caused by the finite-order approximation is resummed in our calculation, yielding a smooth result.

The rapidity difference is related to the scattering angle in the Collins-Soper frame: tanh⁡(Δ​y/2)=cos⁡θ∗\tanh(\Delta y/2)=\cos\theta_{*} when QTQ_{T} is zero. The cos⁡θ∗\cos\theta_{*} distribution is shown in the lower-right frame of Fig. 15. The difference between the signal and background rates is even more pronounced in this variable, clearly expressing the difference in the spin correlations of the systems producing the photons.

A comparison of QTQ_{T} distributions in the top-left panel of Fig. 15 suggests that the signal versus background ratio would be enhanced if a cut is made to restrict QT>10Q_{T}>10 GeV. After applying this cut, we may again examine the distributions in the rapidity difference of the two photons, the scattering angle in the Collins-Soper frame, and the azimuthal angle distribution of the photons in the Collins-Soper frame. The results are qualitatively similar to those in Fig. 15 and are not shown here. A more efficient procedure to increase the Higgs boson discovery significance is to apply a simultaneous likelihood analysis to several kinematic distributions. Based on the present discussion, we would argue that the resummed QTQ_{T}, φ∗\varphi_{*}, and cos⁡θ∗\cos\theta_{*} distributions are good discriminators between the Higgs boson signal and background in such an analysis.

IV Conclusions

The theoretical study of continuum diphoton production in hadron collisions is interesting and valuable for several reasons: there are data from the CDF and DØ collaborations at Fermilab with the promise of larger event samples; there are new theoretical challenges associated with all-orders soft-gluon resummation of two-loop amplitudes; and continuum diphotons are a large standard-model background above which one may observe the products of Higgs boson decay into a pair of photons at the LHC.

In this paper and Refs. [2, 3], we present our calculation of the fully differential cross section d​σ/(d​Q​d​QT​d​y​d​Ω∗)d\sigma/(dQdQ_{T}dyd\Omega_{*}) as a function of the mass QQ, transverse momentum QTQ_{T}, and rapidity yy of the diphoton system, and of the polar and azimuthal angles of the individual photons in the diphoton rest frame. Our basic QCD hard-scattering subprocesses are all computed at next-to-leading order (NLO) in the strong coupling strength αs\alpha_{s}, and we include the state-of-art resummation of initial-state gluon radiation to all orders in αs\alpha_{s}, valid to next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy (NNLL). Resummation is essential for a realistic and reliable calculation of the QTQ_{T} dependence in the region of small and intermediate values of QTQ_{T}, where the cross section is greatest. It is also needed for stable estimates of the effects of experimental acceptance on distributions in the diphoton invariant mass and other variables.

Our analytical results are included in a fully updated ResBos code [31, 32]. This numerical program allows us to impose selections on the transverse momenta and angles of the final photons, in order to match those employed by the CDF and DØ collaborations, as well as those anticipated in experiments at the LHC. Our predictions are especially pertinent in the region QT≲QQ_{T}\lesssim Q. We show that our results at the Tevatron and at the LHC are insensitive to the choice of the resummation scheme and of the nonperturbative functions required by the integration into the region of large impact parameter.

The published collider data are presented in the form of singly differential distributions. We follow suit in order to make comparisons, and we find excellent agreement with data, as shown in Sec. III. We recommend that more differential studies be made, and, to motivate these, we present predictions for the changes expected in the QTQ_{T} distribution as a function of mass QQ, and for the dependence of the mean transverse momentum on QQ.

We make predictions for continuum diphoton mass, transverse momentum, and angular distributions at the energy of the LHC. Moreover, we contrast in Fig. 15 the shapes of some of these distributions with those expected from the decay of a Higgs boson. The distinct features of the signal and background suggest that that the Higgs boson discovery significance can be increased via a simultaneous likelihood analysis of several kinematic distributions, particularly the resummed QTQ_{T}, φ∗\varphi_{*}, and cos⁡θ∗\cos\theta_{*} distributions.

Another approach to the computation of continuum diphoton production is presented by the DIPHOX collaboration [14]. This calculation includes both the direct production of photons from hard-scattering processes and the photons produced from fragmentation of (anti-)quarks or gluons. It is valid at NLO, except for the g​ggg subprocess, which is included at leading order only. The DIPHOX code is useful for rates integrated over transverse momentum, but it is not designed to predict the transverse momentum distribution or other distributions sensitive to the region in which the transverse momentum of the diphoton pair is small. Compared to a fixed-order calculation, such as direct photon pair calculation in DIPHOX, our calculation improves the theoretical prediction for event distributions which are sensitive to the region of low QTQ_{T}. Furthermore, our calculation includes the NLO contribution from the combined g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} channel, leading to more accurate predictions at the LHC, where the g​g+g​qSgg+gq_{S} contribution is generally not small.

Only isolated, not inclusive, photons are identified experimentally. While it is straightforward to define an isolated photon in a given experiment, it is challenging to devise a theoretical prescription that can match the experimental definition, short of first understanding the long-distance dynamics of QCD. The isolated diphoton production rate is modeled in the DIPHOX code by including explicit photon fragmentation function contributions at NLO accuracy. A shortcoming of this approach (as well as of our method for treating isolation) is that one cannot accurately represent photon fragmentation without including final-state parton showering in the presence of isolation constraints. There is inevitable ambiguity and uncertainty in the choice of the “isolation energy” used to define an isolated photon theoretically for comparison with the isolated photon measured experimentally. As shown in Sec. III, the DIPHOX cross section can vary by a large factor in some regions of phase space at the Tevatron when ETi​s​oE_{T}^{iso} is changed from 1 GeV to 4 GeV.

Our approach is to concentrate on physical observables which are less sensitive to the fragmentation contributions. We apply the “collinear subtraction” prescription or the “smooth-cone isolation” prescription to define an isolated photon in our calculation. We find good agreement with the data, except in the region with small QQ and Δ​φ<π/2\Delta\varphi<\pi/2, consistent with our theoretical expectation that higher-order direct photon production and photon fragmentation contributions can strongly modify the rate of diphoton pairs in this region. We suggest that much better agreement with current and future data will be obtained if an addition requirement of QT<QQ_{T}<Q is applied. With this cut, the fragmentation contributions are largely suppressed. With the cut QT<QQ_{T}<Q cut applied to the Tevatron data, the enhancement at low Δ​φ\Delta\varphi and intermediate QTQ_{T} (the shoulder region) should disappear. We urge the CDF and DØ  collaborations to apply these cuts in future analyses of the diphoton data.

In our calculation, we identify an interesting spin-flip contribution (with cos⁡2​φ∗\cos 2\varphi_{*} dependence) in the g​ggg channel, cf. Ref. [3], and we suggest that measurements be made of the distribution of φ∗\varphi_{*} as a function of QTQ_{T}. All-orders resummation of the gluon spin-flip contribution may be needed when a larger statistical sample of diphoton data is available.

The contributions from q​g+q¯​gqg+{\bar{q}}g processes become more important at the LHC than at the Tevatron, and calculations at a higher order of precision may be warranted eventually. To improve the theoretical prediction in the region of phase space with QT<ETi​s​oQ_{T}<E_{T}^{iso} and φ∗∼0\varphi_{*}\sim 0 or π\pi, a joint resummation calculation is needed in which the effects of both the initial- and final-state multiple parton emissions are treated simultaneously.

Although we emphasize that better agreement of our predictions with data should be apparent if the selection QT<QQ_{T}<Q is made, we also point out that the region QT>QQ_{T}>Q should manifest very interesting physics of a different sort. Additional logarithmic singularities of the form log⁡(Q/QT)\log(Q/Q_{T}) are encountered in the region QT≫QQ_{T}\gg Q. These logarithms are associated with the fragmentation of a parton carrying large transverse momentum QTQ_{T} into a system of small invariant mass QQ [27, 28], a light γ​γ\gamma\gamma pair in our case. Small-QQ γ​γ\gamma\gamma fragmentation of this kind is not implemented yet in theoretical models. Experimental study of the region QT≫QQ_{T}\gg Q may offer the opportunity to measure the parton to two-photon fragmentation function Dγ​γ​(z1,z2)D_{\gamma\gamma}(z_{1},z_{2}).
